drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What kind of breathing problem are you having: cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, noisy breathing, or coughing up phlegm?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main respiratory complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: Are you short of breath even when sitting still, or only when you move around or exert yourself?
questions.rationale: Dyspnea at rest suggests more severe disease than exertional dyspnea.

questions.text: Did the shortness of breath come on suddenly, over hours or days, or over weeks to months?
questions.rationale: Onset tempo helps separate acute causes such as PE or pneumothorax from chronic disease.

questions.text: Can you speak in full sentences without stopping to catch your breath?
questions.rationale: Inability to speak full sentences is a bedside marker of severe respiratory distress.

questions.text: Have your lips or fingertips looked blue or gray, or have you felt unusually drowsy or confused?
questions.rationale: Cyanosis or altered mentation can indicate significant hypoxia.

questions.text: How long have you had the cough, and is it dry or does it bring up phlegm?
questions.rationale: Duration and type of cough separate acute infection from subacute and chronic causes.

questions.text: What color is the phlegm, and how much are you bringing up each day?
questions.rationale: Purulent or large-volume sputum suggests bacterial infection or bronchiectasis.

questions.text: Have you coughed up any blood or pink, frothy phlegm?
questions.rationale: Hemoptysis can indicate infection, PE, malignancy, or heart failure and needs prompt assessment.

questions.text: Do you hear or feel wheezing or whistling when you breathe, and is it worse at night or with triggers?
questions.rationale: Wheeze with triggers points toward asthma or reactive airway disease.

questions.text: Is there a harsh, high-pitched noise when you breathe in, or did this start after choking on food or an object?
questions.rationale: Stridor or aspiration suggests upper airway obstruction, which is an emergency.

questions.text: Do you have chest pain that gets worse when you take a deep breath or cough?
questions.rationale: Pleuritic pain can point to pleurisy, pneumonia, pneumothorax, or pulmonary embolism.

questions.text: Have you had fever, chills, or sweats along with the breathing symptoms?
questions.rationale: Systemic symptoms raise concern for pneumonia or other respiratory infection.

questions.text: Have you had drenching night sweats or unintended weight loss?
questions.rationale: These constitutional symptoms raise concern for TB, malignancy, or other chronic disease.

questions.text: Do you get breathless lying flat, wake up gasping at night, or notice swelling in your ankles?
questions.rationale: Orthopnea and edema suggest heart failure as a cause of dyspnea.

questions.text: Do you have pain or swelling in one calf, or recent long travel, surgery, or immobility?
questions.rationale: These features raise the pretest probability of pulmonary embolism.

questions.text: Have you ever been told you have asthma, COPD, emphysema, or another lung condition?
questions.rationale: Known lung disease is the most common explanation for recurrent symptoms.

questions.text: Do you smoke or vape, or have you in the past? About how much?
questions.rationale: Smoking history drives risk for COPD, lung cancer, and infection.

questions.text: Are you exposed to dust, fumes, chemicals, mold, birds, or asbestos at work or home?
questions.rationale: Occupational and environmental exposures cause many chronic lung diseases.

questions.text: Has anyone around you been sick, or have you traveled recently or been around someone with TB?
questions.rationale: Exposure history helps assess infectious causes.

questions.text: Do you have hay fever, postnasal drip, frequent heartburn, or known allergies?
questions.rationale: Upper airway disease and reflux are common causes of chronic cough.

questions.text: Do you take any ACE inhibitors, beta blockers, or have you started any new medicines recently?
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors cause cough and beta blockers can trigger bronchospasm.

questions.text: Do you have a weakened immune system, cancer history, or take steroids or other immune-suppressing medicine?
questions.rationale: Immunosuppression broadens the infectious differential and raises severity risk.

questions.text: Are you up to date on flu, pneumonia, COVID, and RSV vaccines?
questions.rationale: Vaccination status modifies infection risk.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Severe shortness of breath
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient say they are very short of breath at rest, cannot speak full sentences, or are struggling to breathe?

red_flags.label: Blue lips or altered alertness
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report blue or gray lips or fingertips, new confusion, or unusual drowsiness?

red_flags.label: Coughing up blood
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe coughing up blood or pink frothy sputum?

red_flags.label: Stridor or possible airway obstruction
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe noisy high-pitched breathing in, or choking on food or an object?

red_flags.label: Pleuritic chest pain with clot risk factors
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report sharp chest pain with breathing together with calf swelling, recent travel, or surgery?

red_flags.label: Sudden-onset shortness of breath
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe shortness of breath that came on abruptly over minutes to hours?
